We model the effective per-turn storage synchronization latency \(t_{\text{eff}}\) under a Poisson arrival process of authorization events with aggregate arrival rate \(\lambda\). If the group commit coordinator employs a maximum batch timeout window \(W\) and a maximum batch capacity \(K_{\max}\), the expected number of events amortized by each barrier is:
\[\bar{k} = \min\left(K_{\max},\, \max\left(1,\, \lambda W\right)\right)\]
The effective latency experienced by an individual agent thread comprises two components: the expected queuing wait time in the ring buffer, and the physical duration of the storage barrier:
\[t_{\text{eff}} = \frac{W}{2} + \frac{t_{\text{writev}}(\bar{k}) + t_{\text{sync}}}{\bar{k}}\]
As concurrency scales (\(\lambda \to \infty\)), the queuing window \(W\) can be shrunk toward zero (\(W \to 0\)), allowing the system to achieve the maximum queue depth of the storage controller. The physical barrier cost \(t_{\text{sync}}\) is divided across \(K_{\max}\) events, reducing the per-agent barrier overhead from several milliseconds to single-digit microseconds.
Crucially, group commit preserves the causal ordering invariants of every individual agent trajectory. Let \(\mathcal{T}_A\) and \(\mathcal{T}_B\) represent two independent trajectories running on the same host supervisor. Within trajectory \(\mathcal{T}_A\), the sequence of events is strictly causal:
\[e_{A, \text{prop}} \prec e_{A, \text{auth}} \prec e_{A, \text{flush}} \prec a_{A, \text{ext}}\]
The fact that \(e_{A, \text{flush}}\) and \(e_{B, \text{flush}}\) were physically written to flash within the exact same NVMe block write does not alter the causal independence of \(\mathcal{T}_A\) and \(\mathcal{T}_B\). Because neither thread dispatches its network RPC until the shared storage barrier completes, neither trajectory can produce a phantom mutation in the physical world.
Strict adherence to the Write-Ahead Logging invariant guarantees that upon crash recovery, the reconstruction engine possesses an unbroken, mathematically sound audit trail: every external mutation surviving in the real world corresponds to a committed authorization record on disk. However, as an agent trajectory progresses through hundreds or thousands of steps, the size of this append-only log expands monotonically. Rebuilding the operational Agent Control Block (\(\text{ACB}\)) after an unexpected crash by sequentially reading and evaluating thousands of historical events from turn zero introduces unacceptable recovery latency. How an agent supervisor bounds this recovery overhead without incurring continuous disk write amplification is the governing question of periodic state checkpointing.

title: Trajectory Persistence
text:
A pure Write-Ahead Logging architecture guarantees safety under sudden process termination, but it exposes the runtime to a severe computational bottleneck during crash recovery: replay latency scales linearly with trajectory length. If an autonomous coding agent fails at turn \(t = 1{,}200\) after six hours of continuous tool execution, forcing the supervisor to sequentially parse, deserialize, and project twelve hundred historical event records across an empty memory space guarantees unacceptable service unavailability. The recovery engine must reconstruct the active prompt context, the tool dispatch table, the variable environment, and the workspace filesystem state before the neural inference loop can generate a single replacement token. As trajectories stretch across thousands of discrete interaction turns, sequential event-log scan time balloons from tens of milliseconds into dozens of seconds, during which client connections stall and downstream orchestration pipelines idle.
Durable state checkpointing bounds recovery latency by decoupling trajectory restart time from total execution history. By periodically committing a consolidated snapshot of the runtime’s memory structures and filesystem state to non-volatile storage, the agent supervisor transforms crash recovery from an \(\mathcal{O}(t)\) scan over the entire lifetime of the trajectory into an \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) base-state hydration followed by an \(\mathcal{O}(k)\) scan over the short delta log accumulated since the most recent checkpoint. Yet state checkpointing is not free; capturing and committing an operational snapshot consumes host CPU cycles, saturates memory bus bandwidth, and triggers non-volatile storage write amplification that stalls active token processing. A dependable agent runtime must therefore formulate checkpoint cadence as an analytical optimization problem, balancing the immediate write overhead of periodic snapshots against the probabilistic recomputation cost incurred when a crash forces historical trajectory replay.






Figure 4: Periodic Checkpoint Cadence and Replay Recovery: Macro architecture of periodic base snapshots and incremental delta segments (top), contrasting fast bounded recovery (\(38.2\text{ ms}\)) against unbounded re-execution (\(17.5\text{ min}\)), paired with the Young-Daly analytical optimization curve (bottom) balancing snapshot overhead against crash recovery cost.



As demonstrated in figure 4, this operational trade-off governs the macro-architecture of trajectory recovery across two coupled dimensions:

Tiered Checkpoint Tree (panel A): The runtime anchors execution to periodic base snapshots (\(\mathbf{S}_0, \mathbf{S}_{50}, \mathbf{S}_{100}\)) while accumulating lightweight incremental delta log segments (\(\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_k\)) in between. If a process crash occurs at turn 92, the recovery manager does not restart execution from genesis—which would require an unbounded \(17.5\text{ minutes}\) of non-deterministic autoregressive token generation across remote GPUs. Instead, the runtime hydrates base snapshot \(\mathbf{S}_{50}\) and sequentially applies the 42 committed deltas through the deterministic transition function \(\delta()\), restoring active state in just \(38.2\text{ ms}\).
Young-Daly Cadence Optimization (panel B): The analytical curve balances snapshot serialization overhead against the expected cost of crash recovery. The optimal checkpoint interval satisfies \(T_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \cdot \delta_{\text{snap}} \cdot \text{MTBF}}\), where \(\delta_{\text{snap}}\) is the snapshot commit latency and \(\text{MTBF}\) is the Mean Time Between Failures. On high-IOPS local NVMe solid-state drives (\(\delta_{\text{snap}} \approx 12\text{ ms}\)), the minimum of the U-shaped total operational cost curve occurs at a tight cadence (\(T_{\text{opt}} \approx 2\text{ turns}\)); on high-latency cloud object storage (\(\delta_{\text{snap}} \approx 2.4\text{ s}\)), the optimal interval widens to \(T_{\text{opt}} \approx 30\text{ turns}\) to prevent write amplification from stalling the inference pipeline.



Every state snapshot must preserve enough structural information to resurrect an operational Agent Control Block (\(\text{ACB}\)) without re-evaluating historical intermediate events. In an unprivileged agent architecture operating under Zero Ambient Authority (\(A=0\)), the active state vector at turn \(t\), denoted \(\mathbf{S}_t\), comprises three distinct system layers: the supervisor control plane, the structured interaction context, and the external execution environment. The supervisor control plane encompasses the task goal specification, the active step counter \(t\), the remaining token and monetary budgets, the tool authorization capability table, and the lifecycle status of all child subagent processes. The interaction context encapsulates the logical prompt conversation buffer, the active system instructions, and the ordered sequence of validated tool call invocations paired with their returned observation references. The execution environment state captures the guest filesystem mount configuration, working directory pointers, exported shell environment variables, and cryptographic hashes of modified workspace artifacts.
The architectural dilemma lies in how this compound state vector is serialized and committed to disk. The runtime can execute a full state snapshot, serializing the entire consolidated \(\mathbf{S}_t\) into a self-contained, monolithic binary payload, or it can emit an incremental delta snapshot, recording only the differential mutations that occurred since the preceding checkpoint \(\mathbf{S}_{t-1}\).
Under a full snapshot policy, the supervisor marshals the complete \(\text{ACB}_t\) into a compact binary representation—typically using a schema-validated columnar format or zero-copy serialization buffers such as FlatBuffers—and writes the resulting byte array directly to the persistence store. The primary advantage of the full snapshot is immediate, decoupled recovery: resurrection requires reading exactly one snapshot record from disk. The runtime performs no historical backwards-chaining. The storage engine can prune or archive all preceding snapshots and raw event logs prior to turn \(t\) without compromising the recoverability of the active state.
However, full snapshots exhibit prohibitive write amplification as the trajectory context expands. In long-horizon reasoning tasks, the interaction context grows monotonically as thousands of input and output tokens, file diffs, and compiler logs accumulate in the conversation buffer. If an agent’s context window reaches \(128\text{ KiB}\) of structured text and metadata, committing a full snapshot every five turns over a five-hundred-turn trajectory forces the storage engine to write:
\[\text{Total Bytes Written} = \sum_{k=1}^{100} k \cdot \Delta_{\text{turn}} \approx 50 \cdot 100 \cdot 128\text{ KiB} \approx 640\text{ MiB}\]
This steady stream of redundant byte serialization consumes storage bus throughput and evicts active pages from the host operating system’s unified page cache, competing directly with the memory requirements of local inference engines and sandboxed compiler toolchains.


Write Amplification Factor (\(\text{WAF}_{\text{snap}}\)): \[\text{WAF}_{\text{snap}} = \frac{\text{Bytes Written to Disk}}{\text{Unique State Changes}}\] For full snapshots over monotonic trajectories, \(\text{WAF}_{\text{snap}} \propto t\), whereas for incremental delta encoding, \(\text{WAF}_{\text{snap}} \approx 1\).
Incremental delta encoding mitigates this write amplification by decomposing the state transition into a compact delta function:
\[\Delta_t = \mathbf{S}_t \ominus \mathbf{S}_{t - \tau}\]
where \(\tau\) represents the checkpoint stride. Rather than serializing the entire conversation buffer and environment map, the runtime records only the newly appended message tokens, the updated budget decrement counters, newly opened file descriptors, and filesystem inodes modified within the window \([t - \tau, t]\). When operating with an underlying append-only Write-Ahead Log, this delta encoding is frequently free: the delta \(\Delta_t\) is isomorphic to the ordered sequence of event records \(\langle e_{t-\tau+1}, \dots, e_t \rangle\) already committed by the WAL engine, as compared across architectures in table 4.

The engineering trade-off of incremental delta encoding centers on crash recovery complexity. Restoring an agent from an incremental scheme requires locating the most recent full base checkpoint \(\mathbf{S}_{\text{base}}\) and sequentially applying the chain of subsequent deltas:
\[\mathbf{S}_t = \mathbf{S}_{\text{base}} \oplus \Delta_1 \oplus \Delta_2 \oplus \dots \oplus \Delta_m\]
If any delta segment in the recovery chain suffers bit-rot, cryptographic signature mismatch, or torn writes, the entire trajectory downstream of the corruption boundary becomes unrecoverable. Robust production runtimes therefore adopt a hybrid tiered checkpointing strategy: the supervisor emits lightweight incremental deltas at high frequency (for instance, following every mutating tool dispatch) and consolidates these deltas into a monolithic full base snapshot at low frequency (for instance, every fifty turns, or after major task milestones). This architecture bounds the recovery chain to at most \(\tau_{\max}\) delta evaluations while keeping steady-state write amplification flat.



Selecting the temporal interval between consecutive checkpoints represents a classical systems dilemma. If the supervisor checkpoints too frequently, the runtime expends its computational budget serializing data structures, locking concurrent queues, and waiting on non-volatile storage barriers, thereby throttling end-to-end agent throughput. Conversely, if the supervisor checkpoints too infrequently, any hardware crash, network partition, or out-of-memory kernel eviction forces the recovery engine to replay a vast log of historical operations. During replay, the system incurs significant recomputation latency and wastes valuable token and compute budgets re-evaluating deterministic operations.

Definition 1.1: Definition 10.1: Young-Daly optimal checkpoint cadenceLet \(\text{MTBF}\) denote the mean time between failures across the execution environment, \(\delta_{\text{snap}}\) denote the snapshot write and storage barrier latency during which agent execution is throttled, and \(\delta_{\text{rec}}\) denote the fixed state restoration overhead upon reboot.
Under a Poisson failure process where crashes occur uniformly at random with arrival rate \(\lambda = 1/\text{MTBF}\), the expected wasted execution time per unit of productive progress is minimized at the optimal checkpoint interval \(T_{\text{opt}}\): \[T_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \cdot \delta_{\text{snap}} \cdot \text{MTBF}} - \delta_{\text{snap}} \approx \sqrt{2 \cdot \delta_{\text{snap}} \cdot \text{MTBF}} \quad (\text{for } \delta_{\text{snap}} \ll \text{MTBF})\] Accounting for second-order recovery recomputation costs and restart latency \(\delta_{\text{rec}}\), Daly’s higher-order formulation yields: \[T_{\text{opt}}^{\text{Daly}} = \sqrt{2 \cdot \delta_{\text{snap}} \cdot \left(\text{MTBF} + \delta_{\text{rec}}\right)} + \delta_{\text{snap}} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{\frac{2\delta_{\text{snap}}}{\text{MTBF}}} - 1\right)\]


To establish the mathematically optimal checkpoint interval, we adapt the classical fault-tolerance models formulated by J. W. Young (1974) and extended by John T. Daly (2006) for high-performance computing systems. Let \(\text{MTBF}\) represent the Mean Time Between Failures of the execution environment, encompassing host hardware faults, container evictions, spot instance terminations, and unhandled sandbox panics. Let \(\delta_{\text{snap}}\) denote the total wall-clock time required to serialize, flush, and confirm a state snapshot to persistent storage, during which active agent execution is paused or throttled. Let \(T\) represent the checkpoint interval (the time elapsed between the completion of one checkpoint and the initiation of the next).
The total execution time of a long-running agent trajectory can be partitioned into three components: useful progress time (\(T_{\text{work}}\)), checkpointing overhead (\(T_{\text{overhead}}\)), and recovery/recomputation waste (\(T_{\text{lost}}\)). Over an extended operating horizon comprising \(N\) failure cycles, the number of checkpoints taken per unit time is approximately \(1 / T\), meaning the fractional overhead consumed by checkpoint creation is:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{snap}} = \frac{\delta_{\text{snap}}}{T}\]
When a failure occurs, it interrupts the system at a random point within the checkpoint interval. Assuming that failure arrivals follow an independent Poisson process with constant rate \(\lambda = 1 / \text{MTBF}\), the expected time of failure occurrence is uniformly distributed across the interval \([0, T]\). Upon restarting from the last committed checkpoint, the runtime must read the snapshot from disk (requiring recovery latency \(R\)) and re-execute the trajectory up to the failure point. The expected time lost per failure is:
\[\mathbb{E}[T_{\text{lost\_per\_failure}}] = R + \frac{T}{2}\]
Because failures occur at rate \(1 / \text{MTBF}\), the fractional waste incurred due to system failures and subsequent recomputation is:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{fault}} = \frac{1}{\text{MTBF}} \left( R + \frac{T}{2} \right)\]
The total fractional overhead \(\mathcal{U}(T)\) across the life of the agent runtime is the sum of the checkpointing cost and the failure-recovery waste:
\[\mathcal{U}(T) = \mathcal{L}_{\text{snap}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{fault}} = \frac{\delta_{\text{snap}}}{T} + \frac{R}{\text{MTBF}} + \frac{T}{2 \cdot \text{MTBF}}\]
To find the checkpoint interval \(T_{\text{opt}}\) that minimizes total overhead, we compute the first derivative of \(\mathcal{U}(T)\) with respect to \(T\) and set the result to zero:
\[\frac{d\mathcal{U}}{dT} = -\frac{\delta_{\text{snap}}}{T^2} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot \text{MTBF}} = 0\]
Solving for \(T\) yields Young’s first-order optimal checkpoint interval:
\[T_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \cdot \delta_{\text{snap}} \cdot \text{MTBF}} \tag{1}\]
Young’s formulation reveals that the optimal checkpoint interval scales with the geometric mean of the snapshot commit latency and the mean time between failures. If storage performance improves such that \(\delta_{\text{snap}}\) decreases by a factor of four, the supervisor should checkpoint twice as frequently. Conversely, if the agent runs in a highly volatile spot-instance environment where \(\text{MTBF}\) drops from twenty-four hours to thirty minutes, the checkpoint frequency must dramatically increase to bound the recovery blast radius.
Daly extended Young’s first-order approximation to account for higher-order effects that emerge when the snapshot commit time \(\delta_{\text{snap}}\) constitutes a non-negligible fraction of the total interval \(T\), and when failures can occur during the snapshotting operation itself. Under Daly’s formulation, the higher-order optimal interval is:
\[T_{\text{opt, Daly}} = \begin{cases}
\sqrt{2 \cdot \delta_{\text{snap}} \cdot \text{MTBF}} + \delta_{\text{snap}}, & \text{for } \delta_{\text{snap}} < 2 \cdot \text{MTBF} \\
\sqrt{2 \cdot \delta_{\text{snap}} \cdot \text{MTBF}} - \delta_{\text{snap}}, & \text{first-order perturbation expansion}
\end{cases}\]
In practice, an agent supervisor does not measure time purely in continuous wall-clock seconds; it measures progress in discrete interaction turns \(t\). Let \(\mu_{\text{turn}}\) represent the mean wall-clock duration of a single agent interaction turn (including foundation model inference, network transit, tool execution, and local validation). The optimal checkpoint cadence expressed in terms of turn interval \(\tau_{\text{opt}}\) is obtained by discretizing the continuous formulation:
\[\tau_{\text{opt}} = \left\lceil \frac{T_{\text{opt}}}{\mu_{\text{turn}}} \right\rceil = \left\lceil \frac{\sqrt{2 \cdot \delta_{\text{snap}} \cdot \text{MTBF}}}{\mu_{\text{turn}}} \right\rceil \tag{2}\]

Example 1.3: Optimal checkpoint cadence on NVMe versus network block storageConsider an autonomous software engineering agent deployed on an ephemeral cloud instance. The agent executes complex multi-file refactoring workflows where each turn averages \(\mu_{\text{turn}} = 12\text{ seconds}\) (dominated by remote LLM inference and local test execution). The environment exhibits an estimated \(\text{MTBF} = 4\text{ hours} = 14{,}400\text{ seconds}\) due to aggressive spot-instance preemption and container host recycles.
The supervisor maintains an \(\text{ACB}\) and execution context that produces a serialized snapshot payload of \(32\text{ MiB}\) per checkpoint. We evaluate two distinct persistence storage tiers:
Tier 1: Direct-Attached NVMe Flash. The runtime writes serialized snapshots to local NVMe storage using direct I/O (O_DIRECT). The storage tier sustains a sequential write bandwidth of \(1.6\text{ GiB/s}\), yielding a snapshot commit latency of: \[\delta_{\text{snap, NVMe}} = \frac{32\text{ MiB}}{1600\text{ MiB/s}} = 0.020\text{ seconds} \ (20\text{ ms})\]
Applying Young’s formula (equation 1): \[T_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \cdot 0.020\text{ s} \cdot 14{,}400\text{ s}} = \sqrt{576} = 24.0\text{ seconds}\] Converting to interaction turns via equation 2: \[\tau_{\text{opt}} = \left\lceil \frac{24.0\text{ s}}{12\text{ s}} \right\rceil = 2\text{ turns}\] On high-speed local NVMe, the supervisor should commit a snapshot every 2 turns. The fractional runtime overhead introduced by this aggressive checkpointing is: \[\mathcal{U} = \frac{0.020}{24} + \frac{24}{2 \cdot 14{,}400} = 0.00083 + 0.00083 = 0.166\%\]
Tier 2: Network-Attached Object Store. The runtime transmits snapshots over a shared gigabit virtual interface to a remote object store. Due to TLS handshakes, multi-part HTTP POST overhead, and network transit, the effective snapshot commit latency rises to: \[\delta_{\text{snap, Network}} = 4.5\text{ seconds}\]
Applying Young’s formula: \[T_{\text{opt}} = \sqrt{2 \cdot 4.5\text{ s} \cdot 14{,}400\text{ s}} = \sqrt{129{,}600} = 360.0\text{ seconds} \ (6\text{ minutes})\] Converting to interaction turns: \[\tau_{\text{opt}} = \left\lceil \frac{360.0\text{ s}}{12\text{ s}} \right\rceil = 30\text{ turns}\] On the higher-latency network tier, the supervisor must back off its checkpoint cadence to once every 30 turns. The total fractional overhead rises to: \[\mathcal{U} = \frac{4.5}{360} + \frac{360}{28{,}800} = 0.0125 + 0.0125 = 2.50\%\] Attempting to maintain the 2-turn cadence over the network store would waste \(4.5 / 24 = 18.75\%\) of all execution time purely waiting on network I/O barriers.


The mathematical model underscores a critical operational principle: checkpoint cadence must dynamically adapt to physical storage capabilities. If an agent runtime detects storage congestion or network interface throttling, it must dynamically scale the interval parameter \(\tau\) upward to prevent checkpoint queuing from starving forward execution progress.



The central architectural failure in naive agent checkpointing implementations is the plane-skew tearing hazard. An autonomous agent is not an isolated in-memory program; it is a distributed composite spanning three decoupled persistence planes:

The In-Memory Supervisor Plane: The live Python/Rust runtime memory space holding the active \(\text{ACB}_t\), call stacks, token buffers, pending futures, and ephemeral capability tokens.
The Relational/LSM Event Store Plane: The structured database (such as an embedded SQLite WAL engine or external PostgreSQL instance) maintaining the append-only event log \(\mathcal{E}\).
The Sandboxed Guest Filesystem Plane: The guest workspace filesystem containing files modified, compiled, or executed by tools (managed via a Linux container namespace backed by an OverlayFS or Btrfs filesystem).

If the agent supervisor attempts to take uncoordinated snapshots of these three planes independently, recovery guarantees collapse. Consider the concrete failure sequence illustrated in the execution trace mapped in table 5.



Table 5: Plane-Skew State Tearing Failure Mode: Sequence of uncoordinated cross-plane snapshots leading to divergent post-crash workspace state.

When the recovery engine resurrects the trajectory from this torn checkpoint, the supervisor attempts to resume execution from turn \(t=42\). The restored \(\text{ACB}_{42}\) instructs the agent to read /workspace/src/compiler.cc or compute a unified patch against it. However, the restored filesystem snapshot reflects the state from time \(t_2\), where the file was already deleted by uncommitted turn \(t=43\). The agent crashes immediately with an unhandled ENOENT (No such file or directory) error. The system has suffered state tearing: the filesystem traveled into the future relative to the supervisor control plane.
To prevent plane-skew tearing, the runtime must enforce coordinated cross-plane snapshot atomicity. All three planes must advance their snapshot boundaries across a synchronized barrier, ensuring that the restored state reflects a globally consistent cut across memory, events, and disk bytes, following the five-phase quiescence protocol in table 6.



Table 6: Coordinated Five-Phase Quiescence Protocol: Ordered synchronization sequence enforcing globally consistent cuts across memory, events, and filesystem overlays.











Quiescence Phase
Coordination Mechanism
Primary Primitives & System Calls
Target Subsystems




Phase 1: Barrier
Drain in-flight RPCs, pause external tool dispatch, and park incoming model token generation.
Atomic barrier synchronization, queue lock
Model gateway, IPC sockets


Phase 2: Freeze
Commit pending transactional buffers to disk and freeze storage filesystem drivers.
sqlite3_wal_checkpoint(), ioctl(FIFREEZE)
Relational WAL, guest filesystem


Phase 3: CoW Fork
Instantiate copy-on-write process memory clone and read-only storage snapshot.
POSIX fork(), Btrfs subvolume / OverlayFS split
Host page table, storage volume


Phase 4: Thaw
Release filesystem locks and unpark agent threads to resume forward execution loop immediately.
ioctl(FITHAW), condition variable broadcast
Sandbox runtime, execution threads


Phase 5: Commit
Stream frozen memory pages and CoW delta blocks to persistent storage asynchronously in background.
Zero-copy sendfile(), asynchronous block transfer
NVMe WAL, cloud object tier






This coordinated snapshot protocol proceeds through five strictly ordered phases:
First, in the Quiescence Barrier Phase, the supervisor pauses the agent’s outer execution loop between interaction turns. It blocks the dispatch of new tool invocations and drains all in-flight asynchronous completions from the model provider. No mutating syscalls may enter the execution pipeline during this phase.
Second, in the Database Flush Phase, the supervisor instructs the event storage engine to flush all uncommitted WAL frames to disk using PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) or an explicit fsync() barrier. This guarantees that the relational event log precisely matches the current turn \(t\).
Third, in the Filesystem Freeze Phase, the supervisor coordinates with the host container runtime to freeze the guest filesystem. On Linux hosts, this is achieved by issuing the FIFREEZE ioctl against the underlying block device or invoking an atomic snapshot against the storage driver:
// Atomic filesystem freeze prior to storage snapshot
int fd = open("/var/lib/agent/sandboxes/sand_042/upper", O_RDONLY);
if (ioctl(fd, FIFREEZE, 0) < 0) {
    perror("ioctl FIFREEZE failed; aborting snapshot");
    abort();
}
While the filesystem is frozen, all pending write operations to the upper directory of the OverlayFS layer are halted, and the kernel guarantees that metadata structures and directory entries remain completely static.
Fourth, in the Copy-on-Write Fork Phase, the runtime captures instantaneous point-in-time references across all three planes:

Memory: The supervisor performs a process fork (fork()) or utilizes userfaultfd memory tracking to capture a Copy-on-Write reference of the \(\text{ACB}_t\) serialization buffer.
Database: The runtime opens a read-only transaction handle or creates a hard-link copy of the flushed SQLite database file.
Filesystem: The runtime creates an atomic Copy-on-Write snapshot of the container’s upper layer using subvolume cloning in Btrfs (btrfs subvolume snapshot), ZFS clones, or by atomically creating a new upper directory branch in OverlayFS.

Fifth, in the Thaw and Asynchronous Commit Phase, the supervisor immediately issues the FITHAW ioctl to unfreeze the guest filesystem, releases the quiescence lock on the tool dispatcher, and resumes active agent processing. The pause time imposed on the agent is strictly bounded by the microseconds required to capture the metadata pointers and CoW branches. A background I/O worker thread takes ownership of the forked memory buffers, database hard links, and disk snapshot directories, serializing and streaming them to the non-volatile persistence tier asynchronously.

War Story 1.1: Empirical failure trace: Crash recovery verification
The following log trace illustrates a dependable recovery sequence executed by an agent supervisor following an unexpected host power failure during a refactoring task:
[04:12:01.102] CRIT host_kernel: Power fault detected; emergency halt.
[04:12:08.431] INFO agent_boot: Initializing supervisor crash recovery subsystem.
[04:12:08.445] INFO agent_boot: Found valid base snapshot 'snap_t250.bin' (Turn 250).
[04:12:08.448] INFO agent_boot: Verifying SHA-256 integrity: 8f4a3c... MATCH.
[04:12:08.452] INFO agent_boot: Rolling back OverlayFS upper layer to 'snap_t250_disk'.
[04:12:08.471] INFO agent_boot: Restoring in-memory ACB from snapshot buffer: 2.1 ms.
[04:12:08.472] INFO agent_boot: Scanning WAL event log from sequence 251 to 258...

[04:12:08.484] INFO agent_boot: Replaying event 254: tool_auth(patch_apply) -> verified ok.
[04:12:08.490] WARN agent_boot: Event 258 torn at EOF; discarding incomplete record.
[04:12:08.495] INFO agent_boot: Recovery complete. State synchronized at Turn 257. Resuming.


By synchronizing the memory structures, database event logs, and sandbox filesystem layers across an atomic barrier, the runtime guarantees that any restored checkpoint represents a mathematically valid cut of the agent’s world. Crash recovery can unpack the memory image, mount the corresponding filesystem snapshot, and immediately resume forward execution without encountering the phantom files, corrupted git trees, or missing file descriptors that inevitably plague uncoordinated logging systems.
Once snapshots and event logs are safely coordinated and persisted, the runtime faces the challenge of re-activating these records following a failure. How the agent supervisor uses this historical record to rebuild the active control block and resume forward execution—without blindly re-executing external tool actions and triggering duplicate real-world mutations—is the governing systems problem of historical trajectory reconstruction.

title: Trajectory Persistence
text:
When a distributed agent supervisor crashes midway through an automated codebase migration or complex cloud deployment, the runtime cannot simply restart the task by resubmitting the initial user prompt and current repository state to the foundation model. If an operator naively re-executes the agent, the autoregressive inference engine samples an entirely fresh trajectory of candidate tokens. The model may generate different tool invocations, attempt to re-clone existing git repositories, overwrite patched files with conflicting syntax trees, or issue duplicate non-idempotent API calls to external services.
Re-running an unprivileged stochastic foundation model is not replay; it is a brand-new computation that forks physical reality. True trajectory reconstruction requires a dedicated replay mode that rebuilds the exact supervisory state—the Agent Control Block (\(\text{ACB}_t\)), active context window, memory escrows, and authorization boundaries—without querying the foundation model or dispatching a single physical tool action. By treating historical event records as an immutable, authoritative input stream, the agent runtime decouples state re-hydration from external inference and real-world side effects.


The distinction between deterministic replay and stochastic re-execution marks the boundary between dependable systems engineering and fragile scripting. During live trajectory execution, the agent operates in an interactive closed loop with its environment, as formalized in figure 5. At each discrete turn \(t\), the host supervisor constructs an inference context from the current control block \(\text{ACB}_t\) and dispatches an autoregressive generation request to the foundation model \(M\). The model outputs a completion event containing candidate tool proposals \(e_{\text{prop}}\). The supervisor evaluates these proposals against its security policies under zero ambient authority (\(A=0\)). Upon explicit approval, it commits an authorization record \(e_{\text{auth}}\) and dispatches the external action \(a_{\text{ext}}\) to a sandboxed environment. The physical world returns an observation \(e_{\text{obs}}\), and the state transition function \(\delta\) advances the control block:
\[\text{ACB}_{t+1} = \delta(\text{ACB}_t, \, e_{\text{auth}}, \, e_{\text{obs}})\]


TTVM and the Separation of I/O In their seminal work on Time-Traveling Virtual Machines (TTVM), King et al. (2005) demonstrated that deterministic replay of an operating system requires logging every external interrupt, disk read, and non-deterministic processor instruction. In an agentic architecture, the foundation model completion and the external environment observation serve the exact same role as hardware interrupts and DMA transfers: they are external entropy sources that must be logged to make forward execution reproducible.

King, Samuel T., George W. Dunlap, and Peter M. Chen. 2005. “Debugging Operating Systems with Time-Traveling Virtual Machines.” Proceedings of the 2005 USENIX Annual Technical Conference (USENIX ATC), 1–15.
If a crash occurs at turn \(t=47\) and the engineering team attempts re-execution by invoking \(M\) over the accumulated prompt, the system relies on the assumption that the neural network will reproduce the historical trace:
\[\hat{e}_{\text{prop}} \sim P_\theta(\cdot \mid \text{Prompt}(\text{ACB}_{47}))\]
This assumption fails almost universally in production systems. Foundation model inference exhibits non-determinism across temperature settings, GPU floating-point reduction orders in parallel matrix multiplication (GEMM) kernels, dynamic KV-cache eviction policies, and upstream model version updates. Even at temperature \(\tau = 0\), differences in batch sizes across serving runtimes alter floating-point summation trees, yielding divergent logits and alternative token sequences.
Furthermore, re-executing actions against the live environment violates basic safety invariants. External tool invocations—such as submitting pull requests, provisioning virtual machines, or modifying database schemas—are frequently non-idempotent. Re-executing a script that runs git commit or aws ec2 run-instances mutates external state, corrupts repository histories, and invalidates the preconditions of downstream steps.



Table 7: Execution and Replay Architectural Comparison: Comparison of inference engine state, tool dispatch behavior, state evolution, input sources, and operational goals across live execution, stochastic re-execution, and deterministic replay.











Operational Dimension

Stochastic Re-Execution
Deterministic Trajectory Replay

Active foundation model (\(M\))
Severed / Stubbed (Zero inference)

Sandboxed execution (\(A=0\))
Severed / Mocked (Zero mutations)

Input Source

Primary Purpose
Problem solving & task completion
Alternative path exploration
Crash recovery, debugging, audit






In contrast, deterministic trajectory replay treats the foundation model and the external environment as severed peripherals. As outlined in table 7, the runtime initializes the supervisor in replay mode, stubs the model inference client, and replaces the tool dispatch boundary with an event consumer. The supervisor reads the historical event log \(\mathcal{E}_{0 \to t}\) and pumps the recorded completions \(e_{\text{prop}}\), authorization records \(e_{\text{auth}}\), and tool observations \(e_{\text{obs}}\) directly into the state transition function \(\delta\).
Because \(\delta\) is a deterministic state machine implemented in the supervisor software, replaying identical inputs produces identical intermediate states \(\text{ACB}_0, \text{ACB}_1, \dots, \text{ACB}_t\). The runtime reconstructs the exact context window, token consumption totals, and memory escrow tables that existed immediately prior to the crash without incurring inference latency or issuing duplicate physical mutations.






Figure 5: Live Trajectory Execution versus Replay Reconstruction Mode: In live execution (top), candidate proposals flow through authorization escrow to sandboxed tools, returning live observations into the context accumulator. In replay reconstruction mode (bottom), the foundation model client is stubbed and external tool transports are physically severed under Zero Ambient Authority (\(A=0\)), allowing historical state to be reconstructed deterministically by streaming recorded events directly into the transition function \(\delta\).



As schematized in figure 5, the runtime enforces two fundamentally different execution topologies between live execution and diagnostic recovery:

Mode 1: Live Interactive Closed Loop (Top Panel): The supervisory process actively coordinates the full external feedback loop. The remote foundation model performs autoregressive token generation across inference servers. Candidate tool proposals (\(e_{\text{prop}}\)) are intercepted and held in memory escrow, evaluated against security authorization gates (\(e_{\text{auth}}\)), and durably committed across the physical WAL storage barrier before being dispatched to the sandboxed execution environment. When external tools return, observation payloads (\(e_{\text{obs}}\)) are ingested to update the Agent Control Block (\(\text{ACB}_t\)) and append context for subsequent reasoning turns.
Mode 2: Deterministic Replay Reconstruction (Bottom Panel): The runtime isolates the supervisor under Zero Ambient Authority (\(A=0\)). The remote foundation model inference client is stubbed, eliminating redundant forward-pass compute costs and bypassing GPU floating-point non-determinism. Concurrently, the external tool transport is physically severed: an active isolation barrier traps all outbound network and subprocess invocations, preventing duplicate side effects in the real world. Instead of consulting live peripherals, the supervisor streams the historical event log (\(\mathcal{E}\)) directly into the pure transition function \(\delta(\text{ACB}_{k-1}, e_k)\), rapidly reconstructing the bit-exact supervisory state \(\text{ACB}_t\) in milliseconds.




Reconstructing a trajectory from an append-only event log requires a two-phase protocol: base state re-hydration followed by a sequential event fold. When recovering a trajectory that has executed hundreds of turns, folding events from genesis (\(t=0\)) introduces unacceptable recovery latency. The runtime optimizes this process by combining the periodic checkpoints established under Write-Ahead Logging discipline with incremental log playback.
Let \(\mathbf{S}_\tau\) be the most recent physical state snapshot persisted at turn \(\tau \le t\), containing the serialized Agent Control Block \(\text{ACB}_\tau\), the active token buffer, and the memory escrow indices. Let \(\mathcal{E}_{\tau \to t} = (e_{\tau+1}, e_{\tau+2}, \dots, e_t)\) denote the suffix of write-ahead log records committed between turn \(\tau\) and target turn \(t\). The reconstruction protocol proceeds through two strict phases:

Snapshot Deserialization: The runtime allocates an uninitialized supervisor instance and deserializes \(\mathbf{S}_\tau\) from non-volatile storage into host memory. This operation re-establishes the base control block \(\text{ACB}_\tau\), restores the logical context window to its exact state at turn \(\tau\), and re-populates the sandbox mount table descriptors.
Sequential Event Fold: The supervisor opens a read-only stream over \(\mathcal{E}_{\tau \to t}\). For each event record \(e_i \in \mathcal{E}_{\tau \to t}\), the supervisor executes the deterministic state transition:

\[\text{ACB}_i = \delta(\text{ACB}_{i-1}, \, e_i) \quad \text{for } i = \tau+1, \dots, t\]
During this folding phase, the supervisor’s tool dispatch engine is replaced with a verification interceptor. If the historical log encounters an authorization event \(e_{\text{auth}}\) containing an action \(a_{\text{ext}}\), the supervisor does not invoke the sandbox RPC client. Instead, it advances its internal program counter and reads the corresponding \(e_{\text{obs}}\) record from the log stream, injecting the historical standard output, exit code, or error message directly into the context accumulator.


The Escrow Invariant During Replay During live execution, memory escrow holds unverified candidate actions until a verification gate passes. During replay, the verification outcome is already known and recorded in the event log. The supervisor’s state transition function \(\delta\) must still execute the escrow transition logic to ensure that internal state machine assertions—such as token budgets, pending proposal counters, and quota allocations—remain bit-exact across the recovery boundary.
If the supervisor’s state transition logic attempts to establish a live network connection or emit an unrecorded tool action during replay, the verification interceptor raises an invariant violation (\(A=0\) breach). The presence of any unlogged side effect indicates that the supervisor’s code has drifted from the version that authored the trace, or that an unrecorded source of entropy was allowed to influence the live control flow.

Example 1.4: Recovery latency and compute savings in trajectory reconstructionConsider an autonomous coding agent that failed at turn \(t = 150\) due to a transient worker node kernel panic. The trajectory maintained an active context window of \(L = 48,000\) tokens. The system recorded periodic checkpoints every \(K = 50\) turns. The nearest checkpoint was taken at turn \(\tau = 100\).
Physical Parameters:

Serialized checkpoint size \(|\mathbf{S}_{100}|\): \(64\text{ MB}\) (includes serialized ACB, tokenizer cache, and sandbox filesystem overlay metadata).
NVMe read bandwidth: \(3.2\text{ GB/s}\) (\(3,200\text{ MB/s}\)).
Event log delta count: \(n = 50\) turns (\(150\) raw events: 50 model completions, 50 authorizations, 50 observations).
Average event record size: \(4\text{ KB}\) (total event log suffix size: \(600\text{ KB}\)).
Supervisor event fold latency: \(0.12\text{ ms}\) per event on an AMD EPYC 9654 host processor.
Upstream inference service characteristics: Frontier model prefill processing rate of \(3,000\text{ tokens/s}\) at batch size 1; average decode latency of \(25\text{ ms/token}\); average completion length of \(200\text{ tokens}\) per turn.

Trajectory Reconstruction Latency (\(T_{\text{recon}}\)): \[\begin{aligned}
T_{\text{snap\_read}} &= \frac{64\text{ MB}}{3,200\text{ MB/s}} = 0.020\text{ s} = 20.0\text{ ms} \\
T_{\text{log\_read}} &= \frac{0.6\text{ MB}}{3,200\text{ MB/s}} \approx 0.0002\text{ s} = 0.2\text{ ms} \\
T_{\text{event\_fold}} &= 150 \times 0.12\text{ ms} = 18.0\text{ ms} \\
T_{\text{recon}} &= T_{\text{snap\_read}} + T_{\text{log\_read}} + T_{\text{event\_fold}} = 20.0 + 0.2 + 18.0 = 38.2\text{ ms}
\end{aligned}\]
Hypothetical Stochastic Re-Execution Latency (\(T_{\text{re-exec}}\)): Re-executing the 50 turns through the live model requires recomputing prefill and generating completions across all intermediate turns: \[\begin{aligned}
T_{\text{prefill\_per\_turn}} &\approx \frac{48,000\text{ tokens}}{3,000\text{ tokens/s}} = 16.0\text{ s} \\
T_{\text{decode\_per\_turn}} &= 200\text{ tokens} \times 0.025\text{ s/token} = 5.0\text{ s} \\
T_{\text{turn\_total}} &= 16.0\text{ s} + 5.0\text{ s} = 21.0\text{ s} \\
T_{\text{re-exec}} &= 50 \times 21.0\text{ s} = 1,050.0\text{ s} \approx 17.5\text{ minutes}
\end{aligned}\]
Conclusion: Deterministic trajectory reconstruction restores the agent control block in \(38.2\text{ ms}\), achieving a speedup of:
\[\text{Speedup} = \frac{1,050.0\text{ s}}{0.0382\text{ s}} \approx 27,486\times\]
Reconstruction completely eliminates \(17.5\) minutes of GPU idle time, saves tens of dollars in API billing, and introduces zero risk of non-deterministic branching or duplicate environmental side effects.





When an autonomous agent exhibits pathological behavior—such as falling into an infinite loop of invalid compiler invocations, exhausting its token budget, or attempting to read unauthorized directories—post-mortem root-cause analysis is exceptionally difficult. In standard software systems, developers inspect core dumps or linear text logs. But text logs from an agent run are deceptive: they reveal what the foundation model produced, but they obscure the internal supervisory control flow, the dynamic context window slicing decisions, and the token budget accounting that triggered the failure.
Brian Kernighan (1979) observed that “debugging is twice as hard as writing the code in the first place.” When debugging software built around non-deterministic neural components, this difficulty compounds exponentially: if the developer cannot reproduce the exact internal control state, the defect cannot be diagnosed.
Historical trajectory reconstruction provides the foundation for non-destructive time-travel debugging. Because the event log records every interaction at the supervisor-model and supervisor-sandbox boundaries, the developer can treat trajectory time as an addressable, scrubbable dimension. A developer can mount an archival trajectory, select any turn \(t \in [0, T_{\max}]\), and reconstruct the exact in-memory representation of \(\text{ACB}_t\).

Definition 1.2: Definition 10.2: Checkpoint-delta time-travel replay
Given a historical trajectory spanning \(T\) turns with periodic base snapshots \(\mathcal{S} = \{\mathbf{S}_0, \mathbf{S}_k, \mathbf{S}_{2k}, \dots\}\) where \(k\) is the checkpoint stride, and an ordered write-ahead log of deterministic events \(\mathcal{E} = \langle e_1, e_2, \dots, e_T \rangle\):
Any arbitrary historical state \(\mathbf{S}_t\) (\(t \in [0, T]\)) is reconstructible without forward side effects via the bounded left-fold operator: \[\mathbf{S}_t = \text{Fold}\left(\mathbf{S}_{\lfloor t/k \rfloor \cdot k}, \langle e_{(\lfloor t/k \rfloor \cdot k) + 1}, \dots, e_t \rangle\right)\] where the replay engine:

Selects the nearest preceding snapshot \(\mathbf{S}_{\text{anchor}} = \mathbf{S}_{\lfloor t/k \rfloor \cdot k}\).
Maps \(\mathbf{S}_{\text{anchor}}\) into a sandboxed, copy-on-write memory buffer.
Sequentially applies exactly \(m = t - (\lfloor t/k \rfloor \cdot k) < k\) transition deltas without issuing external system calls.
Bounds worst-case random access retrieval latency to \(\mathcal{O}(k)\) event evaluations.



Time-travel navigation leverages the checkpoint-delta index. To inspect the agent state at turn \(t = 35\), the debugger locates the nearest preceding snapshot \(\mathbf{S}_{20}\), deserializes the control block, and folds the 15 intervening event pairs from \(\mathcal{E}_{20 \to 35}\). The developer can then execute non-destructive diagnostic queries against the reconstructed state:

Context Window Slicing Inspection: The developer inspects the exact token array passed to the model’s prefill buffer at step 35. This exposes whether critical prompt instructions, system reminders, or tool documentation were truncated or evicted by the context manager.
Dynamic Token Budget Audit: The developer examines the supervisor’s internal token ledger to evaluate whether runaway context growth degraded reasoning performance before the crash occurred.
Escrow and Authorization State Review: The debugger evaluates pending candidate actions \(e_{\text{prop}}\) against the active permission mask, revealing whether an overly permissive regex filter allowed a malformed shell argument to escape into the sandbox.
Hypothetical Branching (What-If Analysis): The developer forks the trajectory at turn \(t = 35\). The supervisor retains historical state up to turn 35, but switches from replay mode back to live execution under a modified prompt template or corrected tool schema. This allows engineers to verify bug fixes against historical failures without re-running the successful early stages of the task.




A critical challenge in the lifecycle of an agent platform is continuous integration and regression testing. When systems engineers modify the host supervisor—such as optimizing the tool argument parser, refactoring the context compaction algorithm, or updating permission schemas—they must guarantee that these changes do not break existing agent behaviors.
Running live integration test suites against actual foundation model endpoints is impractical for CI pipelines. Foundation model APIs introduce high latency, non-deterministic completions, rate limits, and substantial financial costs. A test that passes in one run may fail in the next solely because the model sampled a rare synonym in a tool parameter, causing flaky test suites that undermine engineering velocity.
Trace-driven regression testing solves this problem by using historical trajectory logs as fixed, golden test vectors. In this harness, the runtime reads hundreds of archived production trajectories and feeds the recorded model completions \(e_{\text{prop}}\) directly into the newly modified supervisor logic.
The test harness validates whether the updated supervisor’s state transitions match historical invariants. For example, if an engineer rewires the tool call parser to handle streaming JSON tokens, the regression runner replays historical \(e_{\text{prop}}\) payloads containing thousands of malformed, escaped, or edge-case tool calls observed in production. The runner asserts that the new parser extracts identical tool names, arguments, and validation errors as the baseline implementation, without invoking a single GPU kernel.
=================================== FAILURES ===================================
_________________ test_supervisor_replay_regression[trace_8492a] ________________
[replay_engine.py:142]: InvariantViolation: Tool argument schema mismatch at turn 14
>   supervisor.apply_event(recorded_event)
E   ValidationError: Tool 'edit_file' argument 'patch' failed validation:
E   Expected valid unified diff string, received unescaped markdown code fence.
E   Historical event e_prop (commit: 9f4a12) accepted this payload via legacy regex fallback.
E   Refactored parser (commit: 3b8c91) rejected payload under strict Pydantic parsing.
E   Divergence detected: Trajectory replay cannot advance to state ACB_15.
=========================== 1 failed in 0.04s ==================================
The regression trace above illustrates a practical failure mode uncovered during offline trace replay. A refactored supervisor parser enforced strict Pydantic validation on unified diff strings, breaking backward compatibility with an unescaped markdown format that the historical agent had successfully handled via a legacy regex fallback.
Because the test ran against an archived event log, the failure was identified in \(40\text{ ms}\) on local CPU infrastructure, pin-pointing the exact turn (\(t=14\)) and token payload where the supervisor logic diverged. By decoupling supervisor validation from live model inference, trace-driven regression harnesses provide deterministic guarantees that platform changes preserve operational behavior across real-world workloads.
Trajectory reconstruction succeeds only as long as the supervisor’s state transition function \(\delta\) can faithfully interpret historical event streams. However, when the runtime attempts to execute live trajectories or verify deterministic behavior across different hardware nodes, subtle sources of non-determinism—floating-point reduction order in GPU kernels, dynamic wall-clock system calls, and unseeded pseudorandom number generators—threaten replay fidelity. What systems techniques isolate and eliminate these entropy sources to guarantee bit-exact execution?

title: Trajectory Persistence
text:
Subtle kernel non-determinism forces deterministic replayers to inject logged tool outcomes rather than re-executing actions.
An autonomous software-engineering agent executing a multi-file refactoring task halts unexpectedly at turn \(t=42\) due to an unhandled supervisor timeout. To diagnose the fault, an engineer retrieves the exact model weights, fixes the sampling temperature to \(T=0\), restores the target repository to the identical Git commit hash, and launches an offline reproduction run on a secondary GPU cluster. Instead of reproducing the timeout at turn \(t=42\), the trajectory abruptly diverges at turn \(t=6\): the model selects an entirely different tool call, emits an unescaped shell argument, triggers an early syntax error, and terminates without ever reaching the target failure state. The bug cannot be reproduced, the crash dump is useless, and post-mortem analysis grinds to a halt.
Bit-exact trajectory replay is disrupted by non-deterministic sampling, floating-point kernel race conditions, and dynamic wall-clocks; runtimes must virtualize and record all entropy sources. A foundation model cannot be treated as a deterministic mathematical function \(f(\mathbf{x}) \to \mathbf{y}\) across distinct hardware nodes, kernel versions, or execution passes. In an agentic system, minute non-determinisms at the micro-architectural or operating system layer do not remain localized perturbations; because autoregressive decoding feeds generated tokens directly back into subsequent attention contexts, a single flipped bit or altered token at turn \(t\) propagates exponentially across subsequent turns. Constructing a dependable diagnostic and recovery engine requires systematically identifying every physical source of trajectory entropy, establishing virtualization boundaries to capture ambient nondeterminism, and enforcing observation escrow during replay.


Entropy enters an agentic execution loop through four distinct architectural strata: stochastic inference parameters, GPU micro-architectural scheduling, dynamic host operating system interfaces, and mutable external environments. Operating systems engineers traditionally classify non-determinism into internal software state and external asynchronous I/O; in agentic runtimes, this boundary shifts because the core computational engine—the parallel matrix execution pipeline on hardware accelerators—is itself a major source of internal non-determinism.
The first and most obvious source of non-determinism is stochastic temperature sampling. When an inference runtime evaluates next-token predictions with a temperature parameter \(T > 0\), the decode loop draws tokens randomly from the resulting categorical distribution. Unless the pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) state and seed are explicitly pinned and preserved, consecutive forward passes over identical prompt prefixes yield different token sequences. While pinning the PRNG seed provides statistical repeatability on a single isolated thread, it remains insufficient to guarantee bit-exact execution on modern parallel inference servers.


Floating-Point Non-Associativity Under IEEE 754 arithmetic, addition is not associative: \((a \oplus b) \oplus c \neq a \oplus (b \oplus c)\). In parallel reduction kernels, changing the arrival order of partial sums changes the round-off error in the final floating-point significand.
The second and more pernicious source of entropy arises from floating-point non-associativity in parallel GPU reduction kernels. High-performance matrix multiplication (GEMM) and fused multi-head attention kernels execute parallel reductions across thousands of streaming multiprocessor (SM) threads. As formalized by David Goldberg (1991), floating-point addition under IEEE 754 standards does not satisfy mathematical associativity. In parallel reduction trees where thread warps schedule dynamically based on DRAM bank contention, cache hits, and clock throttling, the exact summation order of partial products varies from run to run. Consequently, even when evaluating an identical prompt prefix at greedy decoding (\(T=0\)), the raw logit values for vocabulary tokens can drift by small floating-point epsilons (\(\sim 10^{-6}\) to \(10^{-4}\)). If the two highest-ranking candidate tokens have logit margins smaller than this micro-architectural drift, the greedy argmax operator flips. A single flipped token alters the key-value context for all subsequent decode steps, leading to complete trajectory divergence within a handful of generated words.

Definition 1.3: Definition 10.3: The three strata of replay non-determinismDuring offline trajectory replay, divergences between recording time \(t_{\text{rec}}\) and replay time \(t_{\text{rep}}\) originate across three distinct architectural strata:

Host OS Stratum (Kernel & Process State): Wall-clock timers (gettimeofday), process identifiers (getpid), filesystem inode traversal order, and thread scheduling interleavings.
Inference Stratum (Floating-Point Hardware & Scheduling): Non-associative parallel summation in GPU GEMM kernels, warp arrival race conditions, compiler target differences, and asynchronous atomicAdd logit drift triggering greedy argmax flips.
Environment Stratum (External Services & Tool APIs): Dynamic network responses, remote server clocks, mutable database state, and nondeterministic external web payloads.

A runtime achieves strict replay fidelity if and only if all three strata are mediated by deterministic virtual escrow buffers, as categorized in table 8.


The third stratum involves dynamic host operating system state leaked into prompts and control structures. Agent supervisors frequently inject metadata into system prompts, tool schemas, or scratchpads: current wall-clock timestamps via time.time(), host process identifiers via getpid(), local file paths, or random correlation identifiers via uuid.uuid4(). When a supervisor passes dynamic timestamps into an LLM context, the model conditions its reasoning on values that can never naturally repeat during subsequent execution. Furthermore, file system iterators that traverse directory trees without explicit collation return directory entries in raw inode order, which varies across file systems, container instances, and operating system kernels.
The fourth stratum encompasses external environment mutation. An agent does not operate in a hermetic computational vacuum; its primary purpose is interacting with external tools, HTTP endpoints, databases, and operating system shells. Between a production failure at time \(t_{\text{live}}\) and a diagnostic replay session at time \(t_{\text{replay}}\), external REST APIs change their response payloads, public search engines update their indices, remote Git repositories accept new commits, and local filesystems reflect intermediate mutations. If the replay harness allows the agent to execute real tool invocations against live external services, the observations returned to the agent will differ from historical execution, instantly invalidating the state trajectory. These entropy channels and their corresponding systems mitigation strategies are categorized in table 8:

To understand why bit-exact reproduction fails on identical GPU clusters under greedy decoding (\(T=0\)), one must inspect the arithmetic pipeline of parallel tensor reduction. During the prefill and decode stages of autoregressive inference, computing the attention score matrix \(\mathbf{S} = \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K}^T / \sqrt{d_k}\) and aggregating value vectors \(\mathbf{O} = \text{Softmax}(\mathbf{S})\mathbf{V}\) requires summing millions of floating-point products across parallel SIMD lanes.
Modern accelerator architectures optimize throughput by utilizing atomic floating-point accumulation instructions (such as atomicAdd in CUDA) or dynamic reduction trees across thread blocks. In an accelerator with hundreds of streaming multiprocessors, the physical completion order of thread blocks depends on dynamic runtime conditions: memory bus congestion, L2 cache bank collisions, temperature-induced frequency scaling, and thread block dispatch scheduling. Because floating-point representations allocate a fixed number of bits to the significand (10 bits for IEEE 754 half-precision FP16; 7 bits for Brain Floating Point BF16), round-off occurs at every pairwise addition.

Example 1.5: Logit flip via non-associative attention reductionConsider an inference pass for a model with vocabulary size \(V = 128{,}000\), hidden dimension \(d = 4096\), and sequence length \(L = 2048\), evaluating the final linear projection layer \(\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{h} \mathbf{W}_{\text{vocab}}\) under BF16 precision. Suppose that for two candidate tokens—Token A (representing identifier "write") and Token B (representing identifier "save")—the exact mathematical dot products before rounding are:
\[\mathbf{z}_{\text{ideal}}[A] = 14.20012, \quad \mathbf{z}_{\text{ideal}}[B] = 14.20008\]
The margin separating the two candidates is \(\Delta = \mathbf{z}_{\text{ideal}}[A] - \mathbf{z}_{\text{ideal}}[B] = 0.00004 = 4 \times 10^{-5}\).
The projection computes \(\mathbf{z}[i] = \sum_{k=1}^{d} \mathbf{h}[k] \mathbf{W}_{\text{vocab}}[k, i]\) using parallel reduction across \(P = 128\) threads per warp. In BF16, the machine epsilon is \(\epsilon_{\text{mach}} = 2^{-7} \approx 7.81 \times 10^{-3}\). In a tree reduction where summation order is strictly fixed, round-off error accumulates deterministically. However, in an unconstrained atomic accumulation pipeline, partial sums arrive out of order.
Suppose Run 1 schedules warps such that smaller partial sums accumulate first, yielding a net rounding perturbation of \(\delta_1 = -2 \times 10^{-5}\) on Token A and \(+3 \times 10^{-5}\) on Token B:
\[\mathbf{z}_{\text{Run 1}}[A] = 14.20010, \quad \mathbf{z}_{\text{Run 1}}[B] = 14.20011 \implies \text{Argmax selects Token B (`\"save\"`)}\]
In Run 2, memory bank conflicts delay thread block 3, altering the accumulation order such that \(\delta_2 = +2 \times 10^{-5}\) on Token A and \(-1 \times 10^{-5}\) on Token B:
\[\mathbf{z}_{\text{Run 2}}[A] = 14.20014, \quad \mathbf{z}_{\text{Run 2}}[B] = 14.20007 \implies \text{Argmax selects Token A (`\"write\"`)}\]
The logit ranking inverts purely due to micro-architectural scheduling jitter. If Token A corresponds to a structured tool call delimiter while Token B triggers standard prose generation, the supervisor’s state transition function \(\delta\) branches into an entirely disconnected control state.


Systems engineers have attempted to enforce determinism at the GPU kernel layer by replacing asynchronous atomic additions with deterministic segmented scan algorithms or fixed-order reduction trees. While deterministic GEMM implementations exist (such as setting CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG=:4096:8 in CUDA environments), they introduce measurable performance penalties. Enforcing deterministic reductions restricts warp scheduling freedom, prevents opportunistic memory coalescing, and disables dynamic load balancing across SMs, imposing a 10 to 25 percent throughput reduction on dense model serving.
More fundamentally, deterministic CUDA flags only guarantee repeatability across runs conducted on the identical physical hardware model with the identical compute capability, microcode version, and SM count. A trajectory generated on an NVIDIA H100 (132 SMs, FP8/BF16 Tensor Cores) cannot be deterministically reproduced at the kernel level on an A100 (108 SMs) or an L40S, because the thread block tiling dimensions and warp partition topologies differ fundamentally. Consequently, relying on GPU-level arithmetic determinism for trajectory replay is an architectural dead end for portable systems.



Because bit-level model determinism cannot be achieved portably across hardware tiers, a resilient agent runtime must apply the classical systems principle of virtualization. Rather than attempting to force the underlying execution hardware to behave deterministically, the supervisor interposes on the boundary between the agent and all ambient entropy sources. This design separates execution into two operating modes: recording mode during live execution, and virtualized replay mode during diagnostic analysis.


Crash-Only Verification Following Candea et al. (2004), systems should treat recovery paths as first-class operational paths. Virtualized replay ensures that post-crash state reconstruction relies on immutable, recorded event streams rather than live environment synchronization.

Candea, George, Aaron B. Brown, Armando Fox, and David Patterson. 2004. “Crash-Only Software.” 9th Workshop on Hot Topics in Operating Systems (HotOS IX).
Virtualizing host entropy requires trapping every nondeterministic system call before its return value can enter the model context or supervisor state machine. As illustrated in the dual-mode systems schematic in figure 6, when an agent process initializes, the runtime injects an interception shim (via an LD_PRELOAD shared library, an eBPF tracepoint probe, or a custom execution runtime sandbox). This shim operates across two distinct operational regimes:
In Mode 1: Recording (Live Execution), shown in Panel A of figure 6, the agent process runs within its supervisory cgroup and issues standard operating system calls. The interception shim intercepts each invocation, forwards it transparently to the underlying host OS kernel, captures the physical return value, appends the observed entropy to the trajectory’s append-only Write-Ahead Log (WAL), and returns the value to the process. This shim intercepts four critical system interfaces:

Wall-Clock Virtualization: Calls to clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME), gettimeofday(), or language-level wrappers (time.time()) are intercepted. In recording mode, the real system time is returned and simultaneously written to the event stream as a side-effect event \(e_{\text{clock}}\). In replay mode, the interceptor blocks access to the hardware clock and returns the recorded sequence of timestamps from the event log, ensuring monotonic and identical time progression.
Pseudorandom Number Generators: Calls to /dev/urandom, getrandom(), or framework-level seeds (random.seed(), torch.manual_seed()) are intercepted. The initial seed and all consumed random sequences are logged. During replay, the pseudo-random stream is regenerated deterministically from the recorded seed.
Identifier Generation: Dynamic generation of UUIDs, process identifiers (getpid()), and socket descriptors is trapped. The runtime replaces random UUID generation with a deterministic counter hashed with the trajectory’s base execution ID: \(\text{UUID}_k = \text{HMAC-SHA256}(\text{TrajectoryID}, k)\).
Filesystem Traversal Collation: Calls to getdents64 or readdir() are intercepted to enforce strict lexicographical sorting on returned directory entries, neutralizing kernel-dependent inode ordering.







Figure 6: Syscall Interception and Host Entropy Virtualization: Dual-mode mediation shim operating under live execution (top) to forward kernel syscalls and record non-deterministic outputs into the WAL, and under deterministic replay (bottom) to trap kernel dispatches and inject recorded values.



In Mode 2: Deterministic Replay (State Reconstruction), shown in Panel B of figure 6, the runtime decouples the agent process from the physical machine under Zero Ambient Authority (\(A=0\)). When the replaying process executes the state transition \(\delta()\) and invokes a system call, the shim traps the call and severs the link to the host kernel, leaving physical hardware completely isolated as an unmutated, idle peripheral. Instead of sampling physical hardware clocks or unpredictable inode tables, the shim reads the next sequential event record from the durable WAL stream and injects the recorded timestamp, random byte buffer, or process identifier back into the process virtual address space. This virtualization guarantees that the supervisor’s state machine progresses along the identical execution trajectory across heterogeneous compute nodes.
While host virtualization eliminates environment entropy within the supervisor process, it does not resolve divergence within external tools. When an agent invokes an external action \(a_{\text{ext}}\) (such as querying an API, executing a database transaction, or running a build script), repeating this invocation during replay risks secondary non-determinism or unintended external mutation.
To neutralize external tool divergence, the runtime implements observation escrow. In recording mode, whenever an external action \(a_{\text{ext}}\) executes, its complete observation payload \(e_{\text{obs}}\)—including standard output, standard error, exit codes, HTTP headers, and response bodies—is flushed to the append-only Write-Ahead Log before being returned to the model. In replay mode, the runtime completely disconnects the external RPC transport. When the supervisor’s state machine reaches the dispatch phase for \(a_{\text{ext}}\), the action is intercepted by an observation mocking engine. The mock engine validates that the proposed action matches the recorded action schema; if valid, it injects the historical observation \(e_{\text{obs}}\) directly from the event log without dispatching network packets or modifying external filesystems.

The realization that bit-exact model re-execution is computationally expensive and fragile across heterogeneous hardware leads to an essential architectural decoupling: Trajectory Verification vs. Model Re-Execution.
When diagnosing supervisor state machines, distributed consensus, or tool orchestration failures, the runtime does not re-invoke the foundation model at all. Instead, it performs trace-driven verification: the recorded tokens and tool proposals are replayed directly from the immutable event ledger into the supervisor logic, verifying that the supervisor’s state transition function \(\delta(\mathbf{S}_t, e_t) = \mathbf{S}_{t+1}\) faithfully reproduces the expected intermediate states.
If an engineer specifically needs to evaluate model divergence across new model weights, quantization schemes, or inference engines, the system runs divergence analysis mode. Here, the model is re-invoked on the historical prompt prefixes, and the runtime computes token-level log-probability divergence (Kullback-Leibler divergence over logits):
\[D_{\text{KL}}(P_{\text{live}} \parallel P_{\text{replay}}) = \sum_{w \in \mathcal{V}} P_{\text{live}}(w) \log \left( \frac{P_{\text{live}}(w)}{P_{\text{replay}}(w)} \right)\]
By establishing strict virtualization boundaries around wall-clocks, trapping PRNG entropy, escrowing external tool observations, and measuring logit-level divergence, the runtime guarantees that diagnostic analysis operates with mathematical precision. An engineer can bisect a failing trajectory, inspect intermediate supervisor state transitions, and verify algorithmic invariants without being misled by floating-point hardware races or drifting external APIs.
Sealing ambient entropy channels transforms an executing trajectory into a closed, self-contained computational state defined entirely by its serialized Agent Control Block (\(\text{ACB}_t\)), its append-only event stream \(\mathcal{E}\), and its isolated sandbox state overlays. Because the runtime no longer depends on static physical host bindings, local hardware clocks, or unrepeatable GPU reduction schedules, an active trajectory becomes fully portable across space and time. If a worker node experiences physical hardware failure, thermal throttling, or spot-instance preemption, the supervisor can detach this serialized state package and reconstruct the running task on a completely different physical machine without loss of execution integrity. How does a distributed runtime coordinate the live migration of an active trajectory across physical cluster nodes without dropping inflight RPCs or duplicating external side effects?

title: Trajectory Persistence
text:
Physical worker nodes in modern cloud data centers are fundamentally ephemeral. Hardware components suffer unrecoverable bit flips, thermal throttling forces hypervisors to throttle clock frequencies, and hyperscale cloud providers dynamically reclaim spot and preemptible compute instances to balance multi-tenant capacity. When an agentic workload executes an extended software refactoring task spanning forty reasoning turns, dozens of test-suite runs, and hundreds of intermediate file modifications, binding the execution lifecycle to the volatile memory and local storage of a single physical machine creates an intolerable operational vulnerability. Terminating a three-hour software migration task because an underlying host received a 30-second eviction notice wastes millions of input tokens, inflates operational costs, and risks leaving external systems in an inconsistent state.
Decoupling an active trajectory’s execution state into a serialized supervisory control block, an append-only event stream, and a copy-on-write filesystem overlay allows the runtime to evacuate and resume a running agent across physical worker nodes without task loss or duplicate side effects. Rather than treating an autonomous agent as an opaque operating system process tied to specific CPU registers and virtual memory page tables, the runtime treats the trajectory as an explicitly factored distributed state machine. By synchronizing this factored state at clean conversational turn boundaries, the supervisor transforms an unexpected hardware eviction from a catastrophic crash into a routine, sub-second live migration.


In hyperscale infrastructure, transient compute instances—offered as AWS Spot Instances, Google Cloud Spot VMs, or Azure Spot Virtual Machines—provide between 70 and 90 percent cost discounts relative to on-demand pricing. For enterprise agent fleets running thousands of long-horizon software engineering, code synthesis, or data pipeline trajectories continuously, operating exclusively on standard on-demand instances imposes prohibitive capital expenditure. However, these steep cost savings come with a strict systems trade-off: instances are subject to involuntary reclamation whenever higher-priority on-demand workloads spike.


Historically, process and virtual machine migration sought to preserve volatile memory bit-by-bit across physical hosts. Clark et al. (2005) pioneered iterative pre-copy memory migration for whole virtual machines, while Nelson et al. (2005) solved network interface and swap re-mapping. In agentic systems, because the underlying neural weights reside remotely in an inference cluster and the agent’s logic is mediated by an unprivileged supervisor, we do not migrate gigabytes of raw process RAM; we migrate the structured semantic state.

Nelson, Michael, Beng-Hong Lim, and Greg Hutchins. 2005. “Fast Transparent Migration for Virtual Machines.” Proceedings of the 2005 USENIX Annual Technical Conference (ATC), 391–94.
Cloud providers notify virtual machines of impending preemption via hypervisor interrupts, metadata ACPI signals, or polling endpoints. As summarized in table 9, the evacuation window \(\Delta t_{\text{evac}}\) granted to the host ranges from two minutes down to a meager fifteen seconds. If the runtime fails to persist dirty state and relinquish network leases before \(\Delta t_{\text{evac}}\) elapses, the hypervisor abruptly issues a hard reset (SIGKILL equivalent), destroying all uncommitted memory and ephemeral NVMe storage.
